r: The migration passed every staging run, which used a 40 GB snapshot seeded with synthetic rows. Forty minutes into production, it failed, because the real orders table held 1.2 billion rows and a decade of drift. The ALTER TABLE added a NOT NULL column with a default. On PostgreSQL 10, that forced a rewrite of the entire heap. The rewrite first waited behind long-running checkout transactions, then demanded an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and every later write had to wait for it. Within ninety seconds, connection pool exhaustion alerts paged on-call, as requests piled up with no way out. Engineers had assumed the default was metadata-only, but that fast path arrived in PostgreSQL 11, not 10. The rollback runbook had never been rehearsed, and it cost another twenty minutes. Staging had misled them by omission. Teams now shadow-migrate against full-size clones, limit DDL with a 5-second lock_timeout, and backfill in batches before tightening constraints. Some call this "expand, then squeeze."
